prompt.context: Our client is a law firm called Poleskey, Tobar, Girolami & Partners (PTG). PTG specializes in commercial property law. It has a commercial property team and a litigation team. It also has a smaller Trusts/Estates team that is engaged by individuals from the firm's various corporate clients. The partnership has asked us to explore the reasons behind the partners' recent drop in profit share, which occurred despite the fact that all attorneys seemed to be working harder than the previous year.
prompt.question: How would you approach this problem?

clarifying_info.a: Partners: $400/hour (unchanged from last year). Attorneys: $300/hour (unchanged from last year).

clarifying_info.q: How many billable hours do partners and attorneys work?
clarifying_info.a: Partners: 1,500 hours this year; 1,400 hours last year. Attorneys: 1,900 hours this year; 1,800 hours last year.

clarifying_info.q: What is the headcount by team?
clarifying_info.a: This year — Litigation: 12 partners, 41 attorneys; Commercial: 20 partners, 51 attorneys; Trusts/Estates: 8 partners, 8 attorneys. Last year — Litigation: 21 partners, 65 attorneys; Commercial: 24 partners, 60 attorneys; Trusts/Estates: 5 partners, 5 attorneys. Note: at the start of this year several partners left to set up a new firm, taking a number of attorneys with them.

clarifying_info.q: How does the firm bill clients?
clarifying_info.a: The firm charges strictly for billable hours worked at the applicable hourly rate. No premiums or discounts are applied and no alternative billing arrangements are entered into.

clarifying_info.q: How busy are the different teams?
clarifying_info.a: The litigation team is extremely busy. The commercial team is busy but coping. The trusts/estates team is managing easily.

clarifying_info.q: What are the firm's total costs?
clarifying_info.a: Total costs last year: $53.2m. Total costs this year: $49m. A cost breakdown chart is available (see exhibit).

exhibits.title: Costs Handout (PTG Partners)
exhibits.shows: A stacked bar chart comparing total costs last year ($53.2m) and this year ($49m) broken down by cost category.

framework: Identify profit per partner = (Revenue - Costs) / Number of partners
Break revenue into drivers: headcount (partners + attorneys) x billable hours x charge-out rate
Assess whether the issue is on the revenue side or the cost side
Compare this year vs. last year across both revenue and costs
Drill into the partner-to-attorney leverage ratio as a key driver

questions.prompt: Calculate total revenue for this year and last year.
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute revenue as (# partners x partner rate x partner hours) + (# attorneys x attorney rate x attorney hours). This year headcount totals: 40 partners (12+20+8) and 100 attorneys (41+51+8). Last year: 50 partners (21+24+5) and 130 attorneys (65+60+5).

math.setup: Revenue = (# partners x $400 x annual partner hours) + (# attorneys x $300 x annual attorney hours)
math.answer: Revenue fell from $98.2m last year to $81m this year, a decline of $17.2m.

questions.prompt: Calculate profit per partner for this year and last year.
questions.guidance: Candidate uses total revenues minus total costs, then divides by number of partners. Should note that both revenue AND costs changed, and must use the correct partner count for each year.

math.setup: Profit per partner = (Revenue - Total Costs) / # of Partners
math.answer: Profit per partner fell from $900,000 last year to $800,000 this year.

questions.prompt: Why did profit per partner drop even though attorneys are working harder and rates are unchanged?
questions.guidance: The root cause is the deterioration of the partner-to-attorney leverage ratio. A good answer goes beyond simply noting that partners left; it explains that the departure disproportionately reduced attorneys relative to partners, worsening leverage. Last year the ratio was 130/50 = 2.6 attorneys per partner; this year it is 100/40 = 2.5 attorneys per partner. Each partner now has fewer revenue-generating attorneys working under them, which reduces the profit pool even though individual hours are up. Simply saying 'partners left' is insufficient — the departure alone could have left profit per partner unchanged or higher if leverage had been maintained.

math.answer: Leverage declined from 2.6 to 2.5 attorneys per partner, reducing the revenue each partner effectively sponsors.

questions.prompt: What does the cost breakdown exhibit tell us?
questions.guidance: Costs fell overall from $53.2m to $49m, largely because wages fell (fewer staff). Most other cost lines are flat or slightly up. Costs are not the primary cause of the profit-per-partner decline; the revenue drop is the dominant driver. The candidate should note this and pivot back to the revenue/leverage story.

brainstorming.prompt: What steps could the partnership take to remedy the situation?

categories.name: Headcount / Leverage
ideas: Hire more attorneys, particularly in the litigation team given it is extremely busy
Target attorney hiring to improve the partner-to-attorney ratio back toward last year's level

categories.name: Pricing
ideas: Consider increasing charge-out rates for partners and/or attorneys
Evaluate whether current rates reflect market rates given the firm's specialization

categories.name: Practice Mix
ideas: Review whether to retain the Trusts/Estates practice: its partner-to-attorney ratio is 1:1 (8 partners, 8 attorneys), far worse leverage than the other teams
Consider the trade-off: removing the service would negatively impact corporate clients who rely on it

categories.name: Operational Efficiency
ideas: Assess whether workloads can be rebalanced across teams to make better use of available capacity
Examine billing practices to ensure all billable time is captured and invoiced

categories.name: Strategic / Client
ideas: Consider whether the departing partners took key client relationships and develop a plan to retain/rebuild those relationships
Explore whether the firm can grow revenue from existing clients in litigation and commercial teams

recommendation: The drop in profit per partner is primarily driven by a deterioration in the partner-to-attorney leverage ratio following the departure of partners and attorneys at the start of the year, which reduced total revenue by ~$17m while saving only ~$4m in costs
The most direct remediation is to hire additional attorneys, prioritizing the litigation team which is currently understaffed and has high demand
risks: Rapid hiring may be difficult in a competitive legal talent market
Removing Trusts/Estates could damage client relationships with corporate clients
Rate increases could make the firm less competitive if not supported by market data
next_steps: Conduct a lateral attorney hiring drive, with priority on litigation
Benchmark charge-out rates against comparable commercial property law firms
Analyze the Trusts/Estates practice in detail — profitability, strategic fit, and client impact — before any restructuring decision
